newsitem.title: USA: U.S. militia members guilty of bombings, robberies.
newsitem.headline: U.S. militia members guilty of bombings, robberies.

text.p: Three anti-government militia members were found guilty on Wednesday of a series of bombings and bank robberies.
After deliberating for nine hours, a federal jury convicted Verne Merrell, 51, Charles Barbee, 45, and Robert Berry, 43, on all counts after a four-week trial.

The men, all of Sandpoint, Idaho, were charged with robbing the same Spokane bank twice in 1996, on April 1 and then again on July 12. Each time the robbers set off pipe bombs a few blocks away, presumably as a diversion.
Prosecutors said the defendants wanted to punish U.S. Bank for supposed usury which they believed was against God's law.
Evidence at trial was that the men belonged to a militia group and had "very fundamentalist religious beliefs," prosecutor Joseph Harrington said.
The men, self-styled white separatists, belonged to a small sect centred in Sandpoint and described themselves as "ambassadors of Yahweh," an ancient Hebrew word for God.

On April 1, a bomb damaged a branch office of the Spokane Spokesman-Review newspaper, which had printed a series of articles about anti-government paramilitary organisations in northern Idaho. Another bomb was left at the bank.

On July 12, a bomb was set outside a Planned Parenthood office, which apparently was targeted because the organisation counsels women on abortion. The bombs did extensive damage but did not injure anyone.

The men were each convicted of eight counts including destroying a building used in interstate commerce, using a destructive device during a crime of violence and armed bank robbery. Sentencing was set for Oct. 6 before U.S. District Judge William Nielson.
The three defendants sat stoically and showed no emotion when the verdict was read.
Harrington said the bombings of the bank and of the Planned Parenthood office carried a mandatory minimum life sentence.
The three defendants testified that they were either at home or travelling when the bombs went off.
Roger Peven, attorney for Barbee, said there would be an appeal. He said the government had no direct evidence of his client's involvement.

The men were being retried on the bombing and robbery charges. At the end of their first trial in April, a jury convicted them of having illegal weapons and stolen vehicles but a mistrial was declared on the more serious charges.

The three men were arrested near Yakima, Washington, in October 1996 by FBI and other law enforcement officers who said they found loaded weapons, grenades, and more than a thousand rounds of ammunition.

U.S. prosecutors entered hundreds of items of physical evidence against the men, including ingredients of bombs found in their homes, letters on the computer with wording similar to threatening letters left at the robbed banks, and weapons identical to those used in the robberies.
But only Merrell could be placed at the scene of the robberies by eyewitnesses.
The three men admitted to holding anti-government views since hearing of the deadly 1993 federal siege of the Branch Davidian cult compound in Waco, Texas.

Barbee said on the stand that: "I felt ashamed I didn't go there. People should have gone there and put a stop to it -- with violence if necessary." He said the federal government was "ruling over us from the point of a gun."
A fourth man, Brian Ratigan, 38, is accused of participating in the July 12 robbery. He was arrested after the other three and will be tried in September.
